first_check.explanation: 18 U.S.C. § 1836 ('Civil proceedings') exists and, as amended by the Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 (Pub. L. 114-153, § 2(a), 130 Stat. 376), provides the private civil action for trade secret misappropriation at § 1836(b). Section 1836 itself was originally added in 1996 by Pub. L. 104-294 (Economic Espionage Act); the DTSA added subsections (b)-(d). Citing the DTSA as '18 U.S.C. § 1836 et seq.' is the standard form; the Seventh Circuit in Motorola Solutions v. Hytera, 108 F.4th 458 (7th Cir. 2024), likewise describes a N.D. Ill. suit under 'the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016, 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b), and the Illinois Trade Secrets Act (ITSA), 765 ILCS 1065/1 et seq.' The statute supports the proposition that a party may assert civil trade secret claims under it.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (b) Private Civil Actions.— (1) In general.— An owner of a trade secret that is misappropriated may bring a civil action under this subsection if the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce. [govinfo, Pub. L. 114-153:] SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the ``Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016''.

first_check.evidence_excerpt: (5) Claiming Privilege or Protecting Trial-Preparation Materials. (A) Information Withheld. Scott, 38 F.4th 608 (7th Cir. 2022), which cites Tax Track Systems Corp. v. New Investor World, Inc., 478 F.3d 783, 787 (7th Cir. 2007) and Rockwell Graphic Systems, Inc. v. Courts evaluate the question of whether efforts to keep information confidential were sufficient 'on a case-by-case basis, considering the efforts taken and the costs, benefits, and practicalities of the circumstances.'"
